page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: Factorise x³ − 8 as a difference of cubes
steps.margin_note: First mark. 8 is 2³, so the denominator is a difference of cubes. Write the identity a³ − b³ = (a − b)(a² + ab + b²) before using it.
steps.memory_tip: Difference of CUBES keeps the same sign in the bracket: a³ − b³ gives (a − b) times (a² + ab + b²), all plus inside.
lines: Putting x = 2 gives 0/(8 − 8) = 0/0, so the denominator is factorised.
We know a³ − b³ = (a − b)(a² + ab + b²)
Put a = x, b = 2, then  x³ − 8 = x³ − 2³ = (x − 2)(x² + 2x + 4)

recall.must_convey: That x³ − 8 = (x − 2)(x² + 2x + 4) by the difference of cubes identity.

steps.why: Both parts are zero at x = 2, so (x − 2) is a factor of the denominator as well. The difference of cubes identity is the fastest way to pull it out, and it leaves a quadratic that is not zero at 2.
common_mistakes: Giving the second bracket as x² − 2x + 4, which is the difference-of-cubes bracket with the wrong sign.

steps.label: Cancel (x − 2) and substitute
steps.margin_note: Second mark. After cancelling, the numerator is 1, not 0 — write the 1 in. The quadratic below is 12 at x = 2.
steps.memory_tip: Cancelling a whole numerator leaves 1 above, never 0.

recall.must_convey: That (x − 2) cancels leaving 1/(x² + 2x + 4), and x = 2 gives 1/12.

steps.why: A limit as x → 2 uses only values of x other than 2, so (x − 2) is not zero and may be divided out. What remains is defined at 2, so substitution finishes the question.
common_mistakes: Writing 0 above after cancelling and giving the answer as 0.
